title: Circulatory & Lymphoid Organs
summary: See how vessels, the heart wall and lymphoid organs are layered and organized to move blood and mount immune defense.

lessons.title: Arteries, Veins & Capillaries

levels.kid:
Your body has a giant system of tubes called **blood vessels**. They carry blood everywhere, like roads carrying trucks full of food and air.

**Arteries** carry blood away from the heart. The heart pushes hard, so arteries have thick, stretchy, muscly walls, like a strong garden hose.

**Veins** bring blood back to the heart. The push is weaker there, so their walls are thinner and floppier. Many veins have little flaps called **valves** that stop blood from sliding backward.

**Capillaries** are the tiniest tubes of all. They are so narrow that blood cells line up single file! Their walls are just one cell thick, so air and food can slip out to feed your body.
levels.hs:
Blood vessels share a basic three-layer plan, called **tunics** (from the Latin for "coat"):
- **Tunica intima**: the inner lining. It is made of **endothelium**, a single layer of flat cells.
- **Tunica media**: the middle layer of **smooth muscle** and elastic fibers.
- **Tunica adventitia** (externa): the outer coat of connective tissue that anchors the vessel.

**Arteries** carry blood away from the heart under high pressure. They have a thick tunica media. Large arteries like the **aorta** are packed with elastic sheets. These stretch when the heart beats and recoil afterward, which smooths the flow. Smaller **arterioles** use their muscle to tighten or relax, which controls how much blood each tissue gets.

**Veins** return blood under low pressure. Their walls are thinner and their openings wider and often collapsed on a slide. The adventitia is usually their thickest layer. Leg veins have **valves** that stop backflow, and squeezing leg muscles helps push the blood upward.

**Capillaries** are about 5 to 10 micrometers wide, roughly the width of one red blood cell. Their wall is just endothelium plus a thin **basement membrane**, so oxygen, nutrients and wastes can pass across.

Example: under the microscope, an artery and its matching vein often run side by side. The artery is round with a thick wall. The vein is flattened with a thin wall.
levels.college:
**General wall plan.** From lumen outward:
- **Intima**: endothelium on a basal lamina, a subendothelial connective layer, and in arteries an **internal elastic lamina (IEL)**, which looks wavy on slides because it recoils after death.
- **Media**: circumferential smooth muscle with elastin, collagen type III and proteoglycans, all made by the smooth muscle cells themselves. Arteries may have an **external elastic lamina**.
- **Adventitia**: collagen type I and fibroblasts. Large vessels also contain **vasa vasorum** (tiny vessels supplying the wall) and **nervi vasorum**.

**Arteries by size:**
- **Elastic (conducting) arteries**, such as the aorta and pulmonary trunk, have a media of up to around 40 to 70 fenestrated elastic lamellae. They act as a pressure reservoir (the **Windkessel effect**).
- **Muscular (distributing) arteries**, such as the radial or coronary arteries, have a prominent IEL and many smooth muscle layers.
- **Arterioles** have one to three muscle layers. They are the main site of **peripheral resistance**, because resistance scales with radius to the fourth power.

**Capillaries**, three types:
- **Continuous**: tight junctions, no pores. Found in muscle, lung and brain; the brain's form underlies the blood-brain barrier.
- **Fenestrated**: endothelial pores, often bridged by a thin diaphragm. Found in kidney glomeruli, endocrine glands and intestinal villi.
- **Sinusoidal (discontinuous)**: wide, irregular lumens with gaps and a patchy basal lamina. Found in liver, spleen and bone marrow.

**Pericytes** wrap capillaries and postcapillary venules, sharing their basal lamina.

**Veins.** **Postcapillary venules** are the main site where white blood cells leave the blood. Medium veins have valves, which are folds of intima. Large veins such as the vena cavae have a thick adventitia with longitudinal smooth muscle bundles. About 60 to 70% of blood volume sits in veins, which is why they are called **capacitance vessels**.
levels.phd:
**Endothelium as an organ.** Endothelial cells sense **shear stress** through mechanosensors, including the PECAM-1/VE-cadherin/VEGFR2 complex, Piezo1 channels and primary cilia. Laminar flow induces the transcription factors **KLF2/KLF4**, which drive eNOS expression and anti-inflammatory programs. Disturbed flow at branch points activates NF-κB instead, which explains why atherosclerosis favors bifurcations. Endothelial **nitric oxide** diffuses into smooth muscle and activates soluble guanylyl cyclase. The resulting cGMP and PKG lower Ca2+ and desensitize the contractile machinery. Furchgott's 1980 discovery that acetylcholine-induced relaxation needs intact endothelium ("EDRF") led to the 1998 Nobel Prize. **Weibel-Palade bodies** store von Willebrand factor and P-selectin for rapid release, and are a classic electron-microscopy marker.

**Junctions and permeability.** Continuous capillaries use claudin-5 and occludin tight junctions plus VE-cadherin adherens junctions. Fluid flux follows the **revised Starling principle**: the endothelial **glycocalyx**, rather than interstitial protein, sets the effective oncotic gradient. Most filtered fluid therefore returns through lymphatics, not by venous-end reabsorption. Fenestrae (around 60 to 80 nm) are spanned by diaphragms made of **PLVAP**. Caveolae, built from caveolin-1, mediate transcytosis. In the brain this is actively suppressed by **Mfsd2a**.

**Smooth muscle phenotypic switching.** Vascular smooth muscle cells are not terminally differentiated. Injury and PDGF-BB downregulate myocardin/SRF-dependent contractile genes such as ACTA2, MYH11 and CNN1. The cells become synthetic, proliferative and migratory. Lineage tracing (Owens lab) showed that many "macrophage-like" cells in plaques are actually derived from smooth muscle. This overturned assumptions built on marker-based histology.

**Arterial versus venous identity** is specified genetically before flow begins: arteries via Notch/Dll4 and ephrin-B2, veins via COUP-TFII and EphB4. Pericyte recruitment depends on PDGF-BB/PDGFRβ signaling. Knockout mice show microaneurysms and a leaky blood-brain barrier, linking pericyte loss to neurovascular disease. **Elastin** (cross-linked by lysyl oxidase) and **fibrillin-1** microfibrils are both needed for the elastic laminae. Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, partly through excess TGF-β signaling.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic histology pitfalls.** Artery and vein are told apart by wall-to-lumen ratio and the presence of an IEL, not by absolute size. Elastic stains such as Verhoeff-Van Gieson or elastic trichrome are essential. In **temporal artery biopsy** for giant cell arteritis, the key findings are a fragmented IEL with granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cells. Giant cells may be absent, and skip lesions are common. That is why pathologists examine long segments at multiple levels. Age-related IEL reduplication mimics healed arteritis. In **CADASIL** (NOTCH3 mutations), small arteries show granular osmiophilic material on electron microscopy and loss of medial smooth muscle.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Cerebral arteries have a well-developed IEL but a thin media, little adventitia and no external elastic lamina, and they course through CSF. This makes them vulnerable to saccular aneurysms at bifurcations, where medial gaps exist. Aneurysm walls show IEL loss, smooth muscle depletion and inflammation. Wall-enhancement MRI, which partly reflects vasa vasorum and macrophage infiltrate, is being studied as a rupture-risk marker. **Cerebral cavernous malformations** consist of dilated capillary-like channels without intervening brain or a normal mural structure. They arise from loss of CCM1-3 combined with gain-of-function PIK3CA, and MEKK3-KLF2/4 signaling is a therapeutic target. **Moyamoya** shows intimal thickening of the distal internal carotid artery.

**Pharmacologic correlates (mechanisms only).** Nitrates and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors act on the NO-cGMP axis. Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers preferentially relax arteriolar smooth muscle; their unopposed precapillary dilation raises capillary pressure, which explains ankle edema. Bevacizumab-type anti-VEGF therapy causes hypertension and proteinuria by impairing fenestrated glomerular endothelium. Drug-eluting stents use antiproliferatives (sirolimus analogs) to block the smooth muscle phenotypic switch that drives neointimal restenosis.

**Frontiers.** Single-cell atlases reveal **zonation**: a continuum of arterial, capillary and venous endothelial and mural states rather than discrete types. **Brain endothelial heterogeneity** in aging, including loss of Mfsd2a and rising inflammatory transcripts, is an active target. Focused ultrasound with microbubbles transiently opens the blood-brain barrier for drug delivery. Open questions include how pericyte contraction contributes to post-ischemic "no-reflow," a topic of real debate between capillary pericytes and arteriolar smooth muscle.

keyPoints: Vessel walls have three tunics: intima, media and adventitia
Arteries have thick muscular or elastic media and an internal elastic lamina
Arterioles are the main site of resistance controlling blood flow
Capillaries are continuous, fenestrated or sinusoidal
Veins have thin walls, wide lumens, valves and a thick adventitia
Endothelium senses flow and releases nitric oxide to relax smooth muscle

test.q: Which tunic of a vessel wall is lined by endothelium?
test.explain: The intima is the innermost layer, made of endothelium on a basement membrane. The media is the smooth muscle layer.

test.q: The aorta stores energy during each heartbeat mainly through its:
test.explain: Elastic lamellae stretch during each heartbeat and recoil afterward, smoothing flow. This is the Windkessel effect.

test.q: Which vessels are the main site of peripheral resistance?
test.explain: Arterioles change their radius with smooth muscle. Because resistance depends on radius to the fourth power, small changes there matter most.

test.q: Brain capillaries forming the blood-brain barrier are of which type?
test.explain: Continuous capillaries have tight junctions and no pores. Sinusoidal and discontinuous are the same leaky type found in liver.

test.q: Fenestrated capillaries are typical of which site?
test.explain: Glomeruli, endocrine glands and intestinal villi need high exchange, so their capillaries have pores. Muscle, brain and lung have continuous capillaries.

test.q: Wide, irregular capillaries with gaps and a patchy basal lamina are found in:
test.explain: Sinusoidal capillaries occur in the liver, spleen and bone marrow, where cells and large molecules must pass.

test.q: On a slide, a vein next to its artery usually shows:
choices: A wall made of endothelium alone
A thin wall and wider, flattened lumen
A thicker media and round lumen
test.explain: Veins carry low-pressure blood, so they have thin walls and wide lumens that often collapse. The wavy IEL is a feature of arteries.

test.q: White blood cells leave the blood mainly through:
test.explain: Postcapillary venules are the main site where leukocytes migrate out of the blood into tissue.

test.q: Why are veins called capacitance vessels?
choices: They hold most of the blood volume
test.explain: About 60 to 70% of blood volume sits in veins, so they act as reservoirs.

test.q: Leg veins contain ___, folds of intima that prevent backflow.
test.explain: Venous valves stop blood from sliding backward, helped by squeezing leg muscles.

test.q: What cells wrap capillaries and share their basal lamina?
test.explain: Pericytes support capillaries and postcapillary venules and help stabilize the barrier.

test.q: Small vessels supplying the wall of large vessels are called vasa ___.
test.explain: Vasa vasorum, meaning vessels of the vessels, run in the adventitia of large vessels.

kidTest.q: Which vessels carry blood away from the heart?
kidTest.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under strong pressure.

kidTest.q: Why do arteries have thick, strong walls?
choices: They sit close to the skin
kidTest.explain: Strong walls handle the hard push from the heart.

kidTest.q: What do valves in veins do?
kidTest.explain: Valves are little flaps that keep blood moving toward the heart.

kidTest.q: How do blood cells travel through capillaries?
choices: In single file, one by one
kidTest.explain: Capillaries are so narrow that blood cells line up single file.

kidTest.q: The tiniest blood vessels are called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Capillaries have walls one cell thick so air and food can pass through.

advancedTest.q: Atherosclerosis favors arterial branch points mainly because disturbed flow there:
choices: Raises KLF2 and eNOS expression in endothelium
Thickens the glycocalyx and reduces filtration
Stops pericytes from attaching to the vessel wall
Activates NF-κB rather than KLF2/KLF4 programs
advancedTest.explain: Laminar flow induces protective KLF2/KLF4 and eNOS. Disturbed flow at bifurcations activates inflammatory NF-κB signaling instead.

advancedTest.q: Lineage tracing in plaques changed interpretation of marker-based histology by showing that:
choices: Pericytes replace the internal elastic lamina
Many macrophage-like cells come from smooth muscle
Fibroblasts derive from circulating red cells
Endothelial cells are the main source of foam cells
advancedTest.explain: Smooth muscle cells switch phenotype and lose contractile markers, so cells that look like macrophages can actually be of smooth muscle origin.

advancedTest.q: Under the revised Starling principle, most capillary filtrate returns to the circulation through:
choices: Uptake into the vasa vasorum of veins
Reabsorption at the venous capillary end
advancedTest.explain: The glycocalyx sets the oncotic gradient, so venous-end reabsorption is minimal and lymphatics return most filtered fluid.

advancedTest.q: Ankle edema with dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers is best explained by:
choices: Loss of tight junctions in continuous capillaries
Reduced lymph flow from smooth muscle relaxation
Venous valve damage causing reflux in the legs
advancedTest.explain: These drugs preferentially relax arteriolar smooth muscle. Unopposed precapillary dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and drives filtration.

lessons.title: Heart Wall, Valves & Purkinje Fibers

levels.kid:
Your heart is a pump made of three layers, like a sandwich.

- The inside layer is smooth and slippery, so blood slides past easily.
- The middle layer is thick muscle that squeezes. It is the strongest part.
- The outside layer is a thin, wet cover so the heart can wiggle without rubbing.

Inside the heart are little doors called **valves**. They open to let blood go forward and snap shut so it can't go backward. That snapping makes the "lub-dub" sound!

The heart also has special wires called **Purkinje fibers**. They carry the "squeeze now!" message super fast, so all the muscle squeezes together, like a team rowing a boat at the same time.
levels.hs:
The heart wall has three layers, which match the three layers of blood vessels:

- **Endocardium**: the inner lining. It is a single layer of flat cells called **endothelium**, sitting on a thin layer of connective tissue.
- **Myocardium**: the thick middle layer of **cardiac muscle**. Cardiac muscle cells are striped (striated), usually have one central nucleus, and branch. They join end to end at **intercalated discs**, which hold the cells together and let electrical signals pass from cell to cell.
- **Epicardium**: the outer layer, also called the visceral pericardium. It has a surface of flat cells called mesothelium, with fat and the coronary arteries underneath it.

The left ventricle has the thickest myocardium because it pumps blood to the whole body. The atria have the thinnest.

**Valves** are thin flaps covered in endothelium with a tough core of dense connective tissue. They have no blood vessels inside them. The mitral and tricuspid valves are tied to the ventricle wall by cords called chordae tendineae.

**Purkinje fibers** are modified heart muscle cells that conduct signals very quickly. Under the microscope they look large and pale, with few contractile fibers. They sit just beneath the endocardium. A real example: when this conduction system is damaged, as in some heart attacks, a person may need a pacemaker.
levels.college:
**Endocardium.** The innermost layer is endothelium on a thin subendothelial layer of loose connective tissue. Deeper lies the **subendocardial layer**, loose connective tissue containing veins, nerves and, in the ventricles, branches of the conduction system.

**Myocardium.** Cardiomyocytes are striated, branched cells about 10-20 µm wide and 50-100 µm long. Each has one or two central nuclei, often with a pale perinuclear zone holding glycogen and lipofuscin, a "wear-and-tear" pigment. Myocytes are linked at **intercalated discs**, which run across fibers in a step-like pattern:
- **Fasciae adherentes** anchor actin filaments at the transverse parts.
- **Desmosomes** resist mechanical pulling apart.
- **Gap junctions**, built from connexin 43 and found on the lateral parts, couple cells electrically so the heart contracts as a unit.

T-tubules lie at the Z lines, which places them less precisely than in skeletal muscle, where they sit at the A-I junctions. Atrial myocytes contain granules of **atrial natriuretic peptide**, a hormone that promotes sodium excretion.

**Epicardium.** This is mesothelium over loose connective tissue and adipose tissue that carry the coronary vessels. The pericardial cavity separates it from the parietal pericardium.

**Cardiac skeleton.** Dense irregular connective tissue rings (annuli fibrosi) surround the valves and anchor the myocardium. They also insulate the atria electrically from the ventricles, so the impulse can pass only through the AV bundle.

**Valves** are avascular. Each has three layers: the **fibrosa** (dense collagen core), the **spongiosa** (loose, proteoglycan-rich tissue) and the **ventricularis or atrialis** (elastic tissue), all covered by endothelium.

**Conduction system.** The pathway runs: SA node, then AV node, then bundle of His, then bundle branches, then **Purkinje fibers**. Purkinje cells are larger than ordinary myocytes, pale-staining and rich in glycogen, with sparse peripheral myofibrils. They conduct at about 2-4 m/s, versus roughly 0.5 m/s in working myocardium.
levels.phd:
Cardiomyocyte ultrastructure is specialized for sustained aerobic work. Mitochondria take up roughly 30-35% of cell volume, and fatty acid oxidation supplies most ATP in adult hearts. Excitation-contraction coupling depends on **calcium-induced calcium release**: L-type Ca2+ channels (Cav1.2) in T-tubules face ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) on junctional sarcoplasmic reticulum, forming dyads. This differs from skeletal muscle, where triads and direct mechanical coupling to RyR1 dominate. SERCA2a, regulated by phospholamban, re-sequesters Ca2+ during relaxation.

The intercalated disc is increasingly viewed as a single integrated **area composita** rather than separate junctions, because adherens and desmosomal proteins intermingle there. Mutations in desmosomal genes (PKP2, DSP, DSG2) cause **arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy**, with fibrofatty replacement of myocardium. Gap junctions vary by region. Working ventricle relies on Cx43, Purkinje fibers express Cx40 alongside Cx43 for high conductance, and nodal tissue uses low-conductance Cx45, which helps produce the AV nodal delay.

Purkinje fibers fire their own automatic rhythm at roughly 20-40 beats/min, far slower than the SA node. Their long action potentials and dense coupling favor rapid, synchronized apex-to-base activation. In ungulates, especially sheep, they are spectacularly large and visible to the naked eye, which is why Jan Purkinje first described them in 1839. In humans they are less conspicuous. Sunao Tawara's 1906 tracing of the AV conduction axis established the anatomical basis of the conduction system.

Heart valves have their own cell populations. **Valvular interstitial cells** are mostly quiescent fibroblast-like cells that can become activated myofibroblasts. Valvular endothelial cells respond to directional shear differently on the inflow and outflow surfaces. Calcific aortic valve disease is now viewed as an active, osteogenic-like process involving RUNX2 and BMP signaling, not passive degeneration.

A long-standing controversy concerns adult cardiomyocyte renewal. Carbon-14 birth-dating (Bergmann et al., 2009) showed renewal of about 1% per year in young adults, declining with age. Earlier claims of abundant c-kit+ cardiac stem cells were discredited and led to retractions.
levels.expert:
Histology underpins several clinical decisions in cardiology and cardiac surgery.

**Endomyocardial biopsy**, usually taken from the right ventricular septum, remains the reference standard for some diagnoses. Examples include giant cell myocarditis (multinucleated giant cells with eosinophils), cardiac sarcoidosis (non-caseating granulomas; patchy, so sensitivity is low), amyloidosis (Congo red apple-green birefringence, typed by mass spectrometry to separate transthyretin from light-chain disease) and transplant rejection. Rejection is graded by the ISHLT system, with ACR grades 0R-3R and a separate antibody-mediated rejection grading using C4d staining. Pitfalls include contraction-band artifact from handling, mistaking a prior biopsy-site scar for disease, and sampling error in patchy processes.

**Myocardial infarction dating** follows a predictable sequence:
- **Hours**: wavy fibers, then contraction-band necrosis if reperfused.
- **1-3 days**: coagulative necrosis with neutrophils.
- **About 1-2 weeks**: macrophages, then granulation tissue.
- **Weeks to months**: collagen scar.

Forensic pathologists use this timeline, and C4d or complement staining can help detect very early injury. Macrophage removal of dead tissue weakens the wall, which is why free-wall rupture clusters around days 3-7.

**Valves**: rheumatic disease shows Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow ("caterpillar") cells, plus commissural fusion. Myxomatous mitral degeneration shows an expanded spongiosa that disrupts the fibrosa. Bioprosthetic valves made from glutaraldehyde-fixed porcine or bovine tissue lack living interstitial cells and eventually calcify. Tissue-engineered and decellularized valves aim to fix this, especially for growing children.

**Conduction tissue**: in transcatheter aortic valve replacement, the His bundle runs just below the membranous septum. Device pressure there explains why new left bundle branch block and pacemaker needs remain common complications. Conduction system pacing (His-bundle and left bundle branch area pacing) exploits Purkinje anatomy to give more physiological activation than right ventricular apical pacing. Purkinje fibers can also trigger ventricular fibrillation, and targeted ablation of these triggers is an active area.

Open questions include how to coax meaningful cardiomyocyte proliferation, for example via Hippo-YAP manipulation, and how to integrate engineered heart tissue electrically without causing arrhythmias.

keyPoints: Heart wall layers: endocardium, myocardium, epicardium
Cardiomyocytes are branched, striated, mostly mononucleated and joined by intercalated discs
Gap junctions in discs couple cells electrically; desmosomes resist tearing
The fibrous cardiac skeleton anchors valves and insulates atria from ventricles
Valves are avascular, endothelium-covered flaps of fibrosa, spongiosa and elastic layer
Purkinje fibers are large, pale, glycogen-rich cells beneath the endocardium that conduct fastest

test.q: Which layer of the heart wall contains the contractile cardiac muscle?
test.explain: The myocardium is the thick middle muscle layer. The endocardium lines the chambers and the epicardium covers the outside.

test.q: Which component of the intercalated disc allows electrical signals to pass between cardiomyocytes?
test.explain: Gap junctions (mainly connexin 43) couple cells electrically. Desmosomes and fasciae adherentes provide mechanical attachment.

test.q: Purkinje fibers look different from ordinary cardiomyocytes because they are:
choices: Smaller, darker and packed with myofibrils
Larger, paler and rich in glycogen
test.explain: Purkinje cells are large and pale, with abundant glycogen and sparse peripheral myofibrils.

test.q: Where are Purkinje fibers located?
test.explain: Purkinje fibers run in the subendocardial layer of the ventricles.

test.q: Which statement about heart valves is correct?
choices: They lack blood vessels in their core
They are lined by mesothelium on both sides
They are composed mainly of cardiac muscle
They are richly supplied with capillaries
test.explain: Valves are avascular flaps of connective tissue covered by endothelium, not mesothelium.

test.q: One function of the fibrous cardiac skeleton is to:
test.explain: The annuli fibrosi block direct conduction, forcing the impulse through the AV bundle.

test.q: Which chamber has the thickest myocardium?
test.explain: The left ventricle pumps blood into the high-pressure systemic circulation, so its wall is thickest.

test.q: Atrial myocytes contain granules of which hormone?
test.explain: Atrial cardiomyocytes store and release atrial natriuretic peptide, which promotes sodium excretion.

test.q: The surface cell layer of the epicardium is called:
test.explain: The epicardium (visceral pericardium) is covered by mesothelium. Endothelium lines the inside of the heart and vessels.

test.q: Cardiomyocytes are joined end to end at structures called intercalated ___.
test.explain: Intercalated discs combine anchoring junctions and gap junctions.

test.q: What cords attach the mitral and tricuspid valves to the ventricle wall?
test.explain: Chordae tendineae connect the valve cusps to the papillary muscles and stop the cusps from flipping back into the atria.

test.q: The dense collagen core layer of a valve leaflet is the ___.
test.explain: The fibrosa gives the valve strength. The spongiosa is loose and proteoglycan-rich.

kidTest.q: What does the middle layer of the heart do?
kidTest.explain: The middle layer is thick muscle that squeezes.

kidTest.q: What do heart valves do?
kidTest.explain: Valves open forward and shut so blood can't go backward.

kidTest.q: What makes the 'lub-dub' sound?
kidTest.explain: Closing valves make the heart sounds.

kidTest.q: Why do Purkinje fibers carry messages fast?
choices: So the heart can rest longer
kidTest.explain: Fast messages make all the muscle squeeze at the same time, like a rowing team.

kidTest.q: The heart has little doors inside called v _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Valves are the heart's one-way doors.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a mutation in a desmosomal gene such as PKP2. Which histologic finding best fits?
choices: Apple-green birefringent deposits on Congo red
Non-caseating granulomas scattered in the septum
advancedTest.explain: Desmosomal defects cause arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with fibrofatty replacement. Granulomas suggest sarcoid and Congo red deposits suggest amyloid.

advancedTest.q: Why does AV nodal tissue slow conduction while Purkinje fibers speed it?
choices: Nodal cells contain more glycogen, which blocks current flow
Nodal tissue uses low-conductance Cx45 while Purkinje fibers use Cx40
Nodal cells have more mitochondria than Purkinje cells
Purkinje fibers lack gap junctions and rely on desmosomes
advancedTest.explain: Connexin type sets gap-junction conductance. Low-conductance Cx45 in the node contributes to the delay, while high-conductance Cx40 aids rapid Purkinje spread.

advancedTest.q: Free-wall rupture after myocardial infarction clusters around days 3-7 mainly because:
choices: Macrophages are clearing necrotic tissue before scar forms
Neutrophils first arrive and release clotting factors
Collagen scar becomes stiff and brittle at this stage
Contraction-band necrosis peaks after reperfusion therapy
advancedTest.explain: Macrophage removal of necrotic myocardium leaves the wall weakest before granulation tissue and collagen add strength.

advancedTest.q: Why do bioprosthetic heart valves eventually calcify and fail?
choices: Their endothelium overgrows and blocks the orifice
Fixed tissue has no living cells to maintain it
They contain living cells that trigger rejection
They are built from cardiac muscle that fatigues
advancedTest.explain: Glutaraldehyde-fixed tissue has no living valvular interstitial cells to maintain the matrix, so it degenerates and calcifies over time.

lessons.title: Lymph Nodes & Lymphatic Vessels

levels.kid:
Your body has a second set of tiny tubes besides your blood vessels. They are called **lymphatic vessels**. They collect extra watery fluid that leaks out of your blood and carry it back home.

Along these tubes sit little bean-shaped stations called **lymph nodes**. Think of them like airport security checkpoints. All the fluid must pass through them. Inside, guard cells check for germs.

If a guard finds a germ, it calls for help. More guard cells crowd in, and the node gets bigger. That is why the bumps in your neck can swell and feel sore when you have a sore throat. It means your body is fighting back!
levels.hs:
Blood pressure pushes some fluid out of capillaries into the spaces between cells. Most of it goes back into the blood, but a few liters a day stay behind. **Lymphatic vessels** collect this extra fluid, now called **lymph**, and return it to the blood near the heart. Without them, tissues would swell, a condition called **edema**.

The smallest lymphatics are **lymphatic capillaries**. They are blind-ended tubes with very thin walls and overlapping cells that act like one-way flaps. Larger lymphatics have **valves** to stop backflow. Lymph moves because nearby muscles squeeze the vessels. All lymph eventually drains into the **thoracic duct** or the **right lymphatic duct**, which empty into large veins in the neck.

**Lymph nodes** are small, bean-shaped filters, a few millimeters to about 2 cm long, placed along lymphatic vessels. Under the microscope a node has:
- a tough **capsule** on the outside
- an outer **cortex** packed with round clusters of B cells called **follicles**
- a **paracortex** full of T cells
- an inner **medulla** with cords of cells and open channels

Lymph enters through several vessels on the curved side and leaves through one vessel at the **hilum**, the dented side. When you have strep throat, B cells in your neck nodes multiply to make antibodies, and the nodes swell.
levels.college:
**Lymphatic vessels.** Lymphatic capillaries begin blind in most tissues. Their endothelium is extremely thin, has a discontinuous or absent basal lamina, and is tethered to surrounding collagen by **anchoring filaments**. When interstitial pressure rises, these filaments pull the vessel open. Overlapping endothelial edges then act as primary valves that let fluid in but not out. In the small intestine, specialized lymphatics called **lacteals** absorb dietary fat as chylomicrons. Collecting lymphatics have intraluminal valves and some smooth muscle. Large ducts such as the thoracic duct have a three-layered wall like a vein, though the layers are less distinct. Lymphatics are absent from avascular epithelia, cartilage, and bone marrow. The CNS was long thought to have none (see below).

**Lymph node architecture.**
- **Capsule** of dense connective tissue sends **trabeculae** inward. A reticular fiber (type III collagen) meshwork made by **fibroblastic reticular cells** supports the interior.
- **Afferent lymphatics** pierce the convex capsule and empty into the **subcapsular sinus**, then trabecular and medullary sinuses. Lymph leaves through **efferent lymphatics** at the hilum, where the artery enters and the vein exits.
- **Outer cortex**: B-cell **follicles**. Primary follicles are resting. Secondary follicles have a pale **germinal center**, where activated B cells proliferate, surrounded by a darker **mantle zone**.
- **Paracortex** (deep cortex): T-cell zone. It contains **high endothelial venules (HEVs)**, lined by cuboidal endothelium, through which naive lymphocytes leave blood and enter the node.
- **Medulla**: **medullary cords** rich in plasma cells and macrophages, separated by **medullary sinuses**.

Sinus macrophages and dendritic cells trap antigen. Dendritic cells arriving from tissues present it to T cells in the paracortex. Activated T cells help B cells at the follicle border, and germinal centers form.
levels.phd:
Lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) arise largely from **PROX1**-expressing cardinal vein endothelium. **SOX18** and COUP-TFII induce PROX1, though non-venous origins also contribute in some organs. LEC sprouting depends on **VEGF-C** acting through **VEGFR-3** (FLT4). LECs are identified histologically by **LYVE-1**, **podoplanin** (D2-40 antibody), and PROX1. Initial lymphatics have discontinuous **button-like junctions** of VE-cadherin. Collecting vessels have continuous **zipper junctions**, a distinction described by Baluk and McDonald (2007). Valve formation requires FOXC2 and responds to oscillatory shear. Lymph propulsion comes from intrinsic phasic contraction of **lymphangions**, the segments between valves.

Nodes are compartmentalized by chemokines. Stromal cells in the T zone make **CCL19 and CCL21**, which attract CCR7+ naive T cells and dendritic cells. Follicular dendritic cells (FDCs), which are stromal and not hematopoietic, make **CXCL13** for CXCR5+ B cells. FDCs hold intact antigen as immune complexes via complement receptors CR1/CR2. HEV homing follows a sequence: L-selectin binds peripheral node addressin (PNAd, recognized by MECA-79), CCR7 is triggered, LFA-1 integrin is activated, and the cell arrests on ICAM-1.

Fibroblastic reticular cells build a **conduit system** of collagen fibers sheathed by FRCs. Gwyer Findlay and colleagues' work, along with Gretz and Shaw's earlier tracer studies, showed that conduits carry small soluble molecules, below about 70 kDa, from the subcapsular sinus to HEVs and T-zone dendritic cells. Larger particles are captured by **subcapsular sinus macrophages** (CD169+), which pass antigen to follicular B cells.

Germinal centers polarize into a **dark zone**, where centroblasts proliferate and undergo AID-driven somatic hypermutation, and a **light zone**, where centrocytes compete for antigen on FDCs and for T follicular helper (Tfh) cell help. Victora and Nussenzweig's photoactivation studies showed that selection depends on how much antigen a B cell presents to Tfh cells.
levels.expert:
**Meningeal lymphatics.** In 2015, Louveau and colleagues (Kipnis lab) and Aspelund and colleagues (Alitalo lab) independently described LYVE-1+/PROX1+ lymphatic vessels in the dura mater. These vessels drain CSF macromolecules and immune cells to the **deep cervical lymph nodes**. Basal meningeal lymphatics near the skull base appear to be major outflow routes, and their function declines with age. In mice, VEGF-C enhancement improves amyloid clearance and the response to anti-amyloid antibodies. Nasopharyngeal lymphatic plexuses provide further outflow routes. How much this matters for human glymphatic-lymphatic clearance, brain tumor immunity, and post-hemorrhage edema is unresolved, and these questions are directly relevant to neurosurgery.

**Node pathology on biopsy.** Reactive patterns help narrow the cause:
- **Follicular hyperplasia**: autoimmune disease, early HIV, or syphilis.
- **Paracortical expansion**: viral infection such as EBV, or dermatopathic change.
- **Sinus histiocytosis**: nodes draining tumors or prosthetic material.

The crucial distinction is reactive follicles from **follicular lymphoma**. Reactive germinal centers are polarized and contain **tingible-body macrophages**, which have engulfed apoptotic B cells. They are BCL2-negative and have high Ki-67. Neoplastic follicles are back-to-back, monotonous, and BCL2+, reflecting t(14;18). Excisional biopsy preserves architecture. Fine-needle aspiration cannot assess it, a common diagnostic pitfall.

**Metastasis.** Carcinoma cells typically arrive first in the **subcapsular sinus**. This is the rationale for **sentinel lymph node biopsy**: mapping with radiotracer or blue dye followed by serial sectioning and immunohistochemistry. Trials such as ACOSOG Z0011 showed that axillary dissection can often be omitted in breast cancer patients with limited sentinel-node disease.

**Lymphatic failure.** Lymphedema after node dissection or radiation remains common. Microsurgical options include lymphovenous anastomosis and vascularized lymph node transfer. Primary lymphedemas map onto the developmental genes: **FLT4** in Milroy disease and **FOXC2** in lymphedema-distichiasis. Tumor VEGF-C/D drives lymphangiogenesis and nodal spread. Nodal fibrosis in chronic HIV degrades FRC networks and impairs T-cell maintenance. Open questions include how much FRC injury limits vaccine responses in aging, and whether therapeutic lymphangiogenesis can be targeted safely.

keyPoints: Lymphatics return excess interstitial fluid (lymph) to the veins; failure causes edema
Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended with anchoring filaments and overlapping endothelial flaps
Afferent lymphatics enter the convex capsule; efferent vessels leave at the hilum
Cortex has B-cell follicles with germinal centers; paracortex is the T-cell zone
High endothelial venules in the paracortex let lymphocytes enter from blood
Medulla has medullary cords (plasma cells) and sinuses; metastases often land in the subcapsular sinus

test.q: Which zone of a lymph node is mainly populated by T cells?
test.explain: The paracortex (deep cortex) is the T-cell zone. Follicles in the outer cortex hold B cells.

test.q: Where does lymph first arrive after entering a node through afferent vessels?
test.explain: Afferent lymphatics empty into the subcapsular sinus just beneath the capsule. Lymph then flows through trabecular and medullary sinuses.

test.q: What keeps lymphatic capillaries open when tissue fluid pressure rises?
test.explain: Anchoring filaments tether the thin endothelium to surrounding collagen and pull it open as interstitial pressure rises.

test.q: High endothelial venules are specialized for:
choices: Carrying lymph out of the node
test.explain: HEVs in the paracortex have cuboidal endothelium that lets naive lymphocytes leave blood and enter the node.

test.q: A pale germinal center inside a follicle indicates:
test.explain: Germinal centers form in secondary follicles when activated B cells proliferate during an immune response.

test.q: Efferent lymphatics leave the node at the:
test.explain: Lymph enters through several afferent vessels on the convex side and leaves through efferents at the hilum.

test.q: Medullary cords are especially rich in:
test.explain: Medullary cords contain plasma cells and macrophages; plasma cells secrete antibodies into the efferent lymph.

test.q: Why do neck lymph nodes enlarge during strep throat?
choices: B cells multiply to make antibodies
Red blood cells pool in the sinuses
Lymph vessels become blocked by bacteria
Fat builds up inside the capsule
test.explain: Immune activation causes lymphocytes to proliferate, especially in follicles, so the node swells.

test.q: The reticular meshwork supporting a node's interior is made mainly of:
test.explain: Reticular fibers are type III collagen, produced by fibroblastic reticular cells.

test.q: What is the name of the specialized lymphatic capillary in intestinal villi that absorbs fat?
test.explain: Lacteals absorb dietary fat packaged as chylomicrons.

test.q: Swelling of tissues from fluid buildup when lymph drainage fails is called ___.
test.explain: Without lymphatic return, interstitial fluid accumulates, producing edema.

test.q: Most lymph eventually drains into the large ___ duct, which empties into neck veins.
test.explain: The thoracic duct drains most of the body; the right lymphatic duct drains the rest.

kidTest.q: What do lymphatic vessels carry?
kidTest.explain: They collect watery fluid that leaks out of blood and bring it back.

kidTest.q: Lymph nodes are like what?
kidTest.explain: All the fluid passes through them so guard cells can check for germs.

kidTest.q: What shape is a lymph node?
kidTest.explain: Lymph nodes are small and bean-shaped.

kidTest.q: Why might the bumps in your neck swell?
kidTest.explain: More guard cells crowd in to fight germs, so the node gets bigger.

kidTest.q: The bean-shaped stations are lymph n _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Lymph nodes filter fluid and check for germs.

advancedTest.q: A small soluble antigen (about 20 kDa) reaches T-zone dendritic cells within minutes, faster than migrating dendritic cells arrive. The best explanation is:
choices: Transport through the FRC conduit system
Direct entry through high endothelial venules
Capture as immune complexes on FDCs
advancedTest.explain: FRC-sheathed conduits carry molecules below about 70 kDa from the subcapsular sinus deep into the T zone. Sinus macrophages mainly handle larger particles.

advancedTest.q: A node biopsy shows back-to-back monotonous follicles without tingible-body macrophages that are BCL2-positive. This most suggests:
advancedTest.explain: Reactive germinal centers are polarized, contain tingible-body macrophages, and are BCL2-negative. BCL2+ monotonous follicles reflect t(14;18) lymphoma.

advancedTest.q: A mouse lacking CCL19/CCL21 would most likely show:
choices: Loss of germinal center dark zone formation
Failure of B-cell homing into cortical follicles
Loss of valve formation in collecting lymphatics
T cells and DCs failing to reach the T zone
advancedTest.explain: CCL19/21 attract CCR7+ naive T cells and dendritic cells to the T zone (paracortex). B-cell follicle homing depends on CXCL13 instead.

advancedTest.q: Sentinel node biopsy assumes carcinoma spreads in an orderly way. Pathologists focus first on the subcapsular sinus because:
choices: HEVs deliver tumor cells to it from blood
Plasma cells there attract tumor cells
Afferent lymph carrying tumor cells empties there
Germinal centers are located inside it
advancedTest.explain: Tumor cells travel in afferent lymph, which empties first into the subcapsular sinus, so early metastases lodge there.

lessons.title: Spleen: Red & White Pulp

levels.kid:
Your **spleen** is a soft organ about the size of your fist. It sits in the upper left part of your belly, tucked under your ribs.

The spleen is like a filter and a guard station rolled into one. Blood flows through it all day long.

Inside, it has two kinds of areas. The **red pulp** is full of blood. It checks old red blood cells, like a quality inspector. Cells that are too old and stiff get caught and eaten up by cleaner cells.

The **white pulp** is where the guard cells live. These guards watch the blood for germs. If they spot one, they sound the alarm and make germ-fighting tools.

So the spleen keeps your blood fresh and safe!
levels.hs:
The **spleen** is the body's largest lymphoid organ. It sits in the upper left abdomen and filters **blood**, unlike lymph nodes, which filter **lymph**. It is wrapped in a tough **capsule** of connective tissue. Supporting walls called **trabeculae** reach inward from the capsule.

Under the microscope, spleen tissue (the **parenchyma**) has two zones.

- **White pulp**: dense clusters of **lymphocytes** (immune cells) wrapped around small arteries. On a stained slide these clusters look like purple-blue dots. White pulp handles **immune defense** against germs in the blood.
- **Red pulp**: a spongy region packed with red blood cells. It makes up most of the spleen and **filters the blood**. It removes old or damaged red blood cells and recycles their iron.

Red blood cells live about 120 days. As they age, they become less flexible. In the red pulp, blood must squeeze through narrow slits between special vessels called **sinusoids**. Healthy cells bend and slip through. Stiff old cells get stuck and are eaten by **macrophages**, the cells that engulf debris.

A real example: people who lose their spleen (**splenectomy**), often after an injury, have a greater risk of severe infection from bacteria with a sugar coat called a capsule, such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. That is why they need extra vaccinations.
levels.college:
The spleen has a dense irregular connective tissue **capsule** (with some smooth muscle) and **trabeculae** that carry trabecular arteries and veins. A reticular fiber meshwork supports the parenchyma. There is no cortex/medulla division and there are no afferent lymphatics. Blood is the only input.

**Blood route.** Splenic artery → trabecular arteries → **central arterioles**, which are ensheathed by lymphocytes → **penicillar arterioles** → **sheathed capillaries**, which are surrounded by macrophage-rich **Schweigger-Seidel sheaths** → red pulp → splenic sinusoids → pulp and trabecular veins → splenic vein → portal system.

**White pulp** has three parts:
- **PALS** (periarteriolar lymphoid sheath): mostly **T cells** around the central arteriole.
- **Lymphoid follicles** (Malpighian corpuscles): **B cells**. These are primary follicles, or secondary ones with **germinal centers** after antigen stimulation. On a slide the central arteriole looks off-center within the follicle.
- **Marginal zone**: lies at the border with the red pulp. It contains marginal zone B cells and specialized macrophages. This is where blood-borne antigens first meet lymphocytes.

**Red pulp** has two parts:
- **Splenic cords (of Billroth)**: reticular tissue full of macrophages, RBCs, plasma cells and other blood cells.
- **Venous sinusoids**: lined by elongated **stave cells** with slits between them. They are wrapped by ring-like ("barrel hoop") basement membrane bands.

**Functions:**
- **Culling**: removal of senescent or rigid RBCs.
- **Pitting**: removal of inclusions such as **Howell-Jolly bodies** without destroying the cell.
- **Iron recycling**: macrophages break down hemoglobin, store iron as ferritin or hemosiderin, and export bilirubin.
- **Immune responses**: to blood-borne antigens, especially encapsulated bacteria.
- **Platelet reservoir**: about one-third of platelets are held in the spleen.
- **Fetal hematopoiesis**.

After splenectomy, Howell-Jolly bodies appear in blood smears. Patients face a risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (**OPSI**).
levels.phd:
Splenic microcirculation is **open** in humans, at least in large part. Most arterial capillaries terminate freely in the cords rather than connecting directly to sinusoids. Blood percolates slowly through the macrophage-rich reticular meshwork. To re-enter the circulation, it must cross interendothelial slits in the sinus wall that are roughly 1 µm or less wide.

An RBC is about 7-8 µm in diameter, so passage demands great deformability. Buffet and colleagues' ex vivo perfused human spleen model directly showed the importance of this. Rigid, poorly deformable RBCs are retained, including heated cells, ring-stage *Plasmodium falciparum*-infected cells and spherocytes. Retention relates mainly to the cell's surface-area-to-volume ratio. This **mechanical filtration** works together with molecular "eat-me" signals:
- loss of the CD47 "don't-eat-me" signal on aged cells, which normally engages SIRPα on macrophages
- phosphatidylserine exposure
- band 3 clustering with bound naturally occurring IgG

**Red pulp macrophages** depend on the transcription factor **SPI-C** for their development; heme induces Spic. They express abundant CD163 and heme oxygenase-1. They export iron via **ferroportin**, which is regulated by hepcidin.

The **marginal zone** in rodents is bounded by the **marginal sinus** and hosts distinct macrophage subsets:
- SIGN-R1⁺/MARCO⁺ marginal zone macrophages
- CD169⁺ marginal metallophilic macrophages

The human marginal zone is architecturally different. It has a perifollicular zone and lacks a clear marginal sinus, so rodent findings transfer imperfectly. Marginal zone B cells (IgM-bright, IgD-dim, CD21-bright) mount rapid, largely T-independent responses to polysaccharide antigens. They also shuttle antigen to follicles.

This explains clinical observations. Asplenic patients are vulnerable to encapsulated organisms such as *S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae* type b and *N. meningitidis*. Infants respond poorly to pure polysaccharide vaccines because marginal zone maturation is delayed until about age 2. Conjugate vaccines bypass this by recruiting T cell help.

White pulp compartmentalization is chemokine-driven. Stromal cells in the T zone produce **CCL19/CCL21**, which act on CCR7. Follicular dendritic cells produce **CXCL13**, which acts on CXCR5. Lymphotoxin-deficient mice lack organized white pulp.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the spleen is read mostly indirectly: in the blood smear, on imaging and on pathology.

Smear signs of hyposplenism or asplenia:
- **Howell-Jolly bodies** (failed pitting)
- target cells and acanthocytes
- **pitted (pocked) RBCs**, visible on interference-contrast microscopy, which can be used to quantify splenic function
- persistent thrombocytosis

**Functional hyposplenism** occurs despite an anatomically present spleen. It is seen in:
- sickle cell disease, where repeated microinfarction in the hypoxic, acidotic, slow-flow cords leads to autosplenectomy
- celiac disease
- graft-versus-host disease

**Splenic sequestration crisis** in young children with sickle cell disease reflects the same red pulp physiology working in reverse. Massive pooling of blood causes acute anemia and shock.

**Splenomegaly** has categories that map onto the histology:
- **Red pulp expansion**: congestion from portal hypertension, extramedullary hematopoiesis in myelofibrosis, work hypertrophy in hereditary spherocytosis or thalassemia, infiltration in hairy cell leukemia, and storage disease, for example Gaucher cells.
- **White pulp expansion**: reactive follicular hyperplasia in infections, splenic marginal zone lymphoma (which may show villous lymphocytes on smear) and other lymphomas.

For surgeons, the pulp is friable and its capsule is thin, which is why the spleen is the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma. Management has shifted strongly toward **nonoperative management** and angioembolization, partly to preserve immune function. Partial splenectomy and splenic autotransplantation remain options in some settings, though how well implants restore filtration is debated. **Accessory spleens (splenules)** are present in roughly 10-15% of people. They can cause recurrence of immune thrombocytopenia after splenectomy, and on imaging they can mimic tumors.

Open questions and recent advances:
- Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are refining human splenic stromal and macrophage maps. These maps confirm that mouse marginal zone anatomy does not reliably model the human organ.
- Microfluidic "spleen-on-chip" slit devices are used to test RBC deformability, relevant to stored transfusion blood and antimalarial drug screening. Artemisinin-induced pitting may help explain **post-artesunate delayed hemolysis**.
- The spleen acts as a reservoir of monocytes that deploy after myocardial infarction (Swirski and colleagues, in mice), which broadens its role beyond filtration.

keyPoints: The spleen filters blood, not lymph; it has a capsule and trabeculae but no cortex/medulla
White pulp: PALS (T cells) around central arterioles, follicles (B cells), and the marginal zone
Red pulp: splenic cords of Billroth plus venous sinusoids lined by stave cells
Rigid old RBCs fail to squeeze through sinusoid slits and are culled by macrophages
Pitting removes inclusions; Howell-Jolly bodies on a smear signal asplenia
Marginal zone B cells fight encapsulated bacteria; asplenia raises OPSI risk

test.q: What fluid does the spleen filter?
test.explain: The spleen filters blood. Lymph nodes filter lymph and receive afferent lymphatics, which the spleen lacks.

test.q: Which cells mainly form the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS)?
test.explain: PALS is the T-cell zone around the central arteriole. B cells occupy the follicles.

test.q: Where in the spleen are aged red blood cells mainly removed?
test.explain: In the red pulp, stiff RBCs fail to pass through sinusoid slits and are eaten by macrophages in the cords.

test.q: The elongated endothelial cells lining splenic sinusoids are called:
test.explain: Stave cells line the sinusoids with slits between them. Kupffer cells are liver macrophages.

test.q: Removing an inclusion from an RBC without destroying the cell is called:
test.explain: Pitting removes inclusions such as Howell-Jolly bodies. Culling destroys the whole aged cell.

test.q: Which blood smear finding suggests that a person has no functioning spleen?
test.explain: Without splenic pitting, nuclear remnants called Howell-Jolly bodies remain in circulating RBCs.

test.q: After splenectomy, patients face the greatest risk from which kind of organism?
test.explain: Organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae have polysaccharide capsules. Defense against them depends heavily on the spleen's marginal zone and macrophages.

test.q: Where do blood-borne antigens first meet lymphocytes in the spleen?
test.explain: The marginal zone sits at the border of white and red pulp, where blood is released near macrophages and marginal zone B cells.

test.q: Why do healthy red blood cells pass through sinusoid slits while old ones get trapped?
test.explain: The slits are far narrower than an RBC, so cells must bend to pass. Aged cells are stiffer and get retained.

test.q: The splenic cords in the red pulp are named after ___.
test.explain: The splenic cords of Billroth are reticular tissue full of macrophages and blood cells.

test.q: What is the surgical removal of the spleen called?
test.explain: Splenectomy leaves patients vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria, so they need extra vaccinations.

test.q: Blood-filled red pulp makes up most of the spleen, while lymphocyte-rich ___ pulp handles immune defense.
test.explain: White pulp consists of lymphocyte clusters around arterioles.

kidTest.q: Where is your spleen?
choices: Inside your chest by the lungs
Lower right side near the hip
Upper left belly under the ribs
kidTest.explain: The spleen sits in the upper left belly, tucked under the ribs.

kidTest.q: What does the red pulp do?
choices: Helps you breathe air in and out
Checks and removes old red blood cells
Makes the food in your belly smaller
kidTest.explain: The red pulp is like a quality inspector for blood cells.

kidTest.q: What lives in the white pulp?
choices: Guard cells that watch for germs
Bone cells that build hard parts
kidTest.explain: The white pulp holds immune guard cells.

kidTest.q: About how big is the spleen?
kidTest.explain: The spleen is roughly fist-sized.

kidTest.q: The spleen filters this red liquid: b _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Blood flows through the spleen all day.

advancedTest.q: Ring-stage P. falciparum-infected RBCs and spherocytes are both retained in the spleen chiefly because they:
choices: Bind CXCL13 released by follicular stroma
Enter closed circulation that skips the cords
Lose deformability for crossing narrow slits
Express more CD47 on their outer membrane
advancedTest.explain: Ex vivo perfusion studies show that retention tracks reduced deformability (surface-to-volume ratio) at the interendothelial slits. Losing CD47, not gaining it, promotes clearance.

advancedTest.q: Why do 18-month-olds respond poorly to pure polysaccharide vaccines but well to conjugate vaccines?
choices: Their marginal zone B cell responses are still immature
Their sinusoid slits are too narrow for antigen
Their PALS lacks CCR7-expressing T cells at birth
Their red pulp macrophages lack the SPI-C factor
advancedTest.explain: T-independent polysaccharide responses rely on marginal zone B cells, which mature around age 2. Conjugation to a protein recruits T-cell help instead.

advancedTest.q: Splenomegaly with marked extramedullary hematopoiesis in myelofibrosis predominantly expands which compartment?
advancedTest.explain: Extramedullary hematopoiesis occupies the red pulp cords. Reactive hyperplasia and marginal zone lymphoma expand the white pulp instead.

advancedTest.q: A patient's ITP relapses years after splenectomy, and no Howell-Jolly bodies are seen. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Germinal center loss in lymph nodes
advancedTest.explain: Splenules restore pitting, which removes Howell-Jolly bodies, and continue clearing antibody-coated platelets. Splenules are a classic cause of ITP recurrence.

lessons.title: Thymus, Tonsils & MALT

levels.kid:
Your body has a training school for germ-fighters. It is called the **thymus**, and it sits in your chest, just above your heart. Young fighter cells called **T cells** go there to learn. They learn to attack germs but leave your own body alone. Cells that fail the test do not graduate.

You also have guard posts at the doors of your body. Your **tonsils** sit at the back of your throat, where food and air come in. They catch germs early and raise the alarm.

Your gut and airways have tiny guard posts too, called **MALT**. They watch everything you swallow and breathe. The thymus is biggest when you are a kid, and it slowly shrinks as you grow up.
levels.hs:
Lymphoid organs come in two kinds. **Primary lymphoid organs** are where immune cells are made and trained: the bone marrow and the **thymus**. **Secondary lymphoid organs** are where trained cells meet invaders: lymph nodes, spleen, **tonsils** and **MALT** (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue).

The thymus sits in the upper chest behind the breastbone. Under the microscope it is split into **lobules**. Each lobule has a dark outer **cortex** packed with developing T cells (thymocytes) and a paler inner **medulla**. The medulla contains **Hassall's corpuscles**, swirls of flattened cells that look like onion slices. They are the classic way to identify the thymus on a slide. Most thymocytes never graduate. Those that cannot recognize anything, or that react strongly against the body's own proteins, die. The thymus is largest in childhood and is gradually replaced by fat, a process called **involution**.

Tonsils form a ring around the throat called **Waldeyer's ring**. The **palatine tonsils** (the ones you can see) are covered by stratified squamous epithelium that dips inward into deep pits called **crypts**, which trap material. Beneath lie **lymphoid follicles** with pale germinal centers where B cells multiply.

MALT is scattered lymphoid tissue in mucous membranes. The best example is **Peyer's patches** in the last part of the small intestine (ileum).
levels.college:
**Thymus.** The thymus is a bilobed organ with a connective-tissue capsule. Septa (trabeculae) extend inward and divide it into incomplete lobules. Unlike lymph nodes it has **no lymphoid follicles**, no afferent lymphatics and no sinuses. Its framework is not reticular fibers but **thymic epithelial cells** (TECs), derived from endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch. TECs join one another by desmosomes into a meshwork.
- **Cortex**: densely packed small thymocytes (dark staining), cortical TECs and macrophages that clear apoptotic cells (tingible-body macrophages). Here thymocytes undergo **positive selection**: those whose T-cell receptor binds self-MHC weakly survive.
- **Medulla**: fewer, more mature thymocytes, medullary TECs, dendritic cells and **Hassall's corpuscles** (keratinized concentric epithelial whorls). **Negative selection** deletes cells that react strongly to self-antigens.
- **Blood-thymus barrier** (cortex): continuous capillary endothelium with a thick basal lamina, pericytes, macrophages and a sheath of epithelial cells. It shields developing thymocytes from circulating antigen.

Mature T cells exit through medullary venules and lymphatics. Involution begins after puberty; adipose tissue replaces the parenchyma, though some T-cell output continues into adulthood.

**Tonsils** are partially encapsulated aggregates:
- **Palatine**: stratified squamous nonkeratinized epithelium, 10 to 20 deep crypts, a dense capsule underneath.
- **Pharyngeal** (adenoid): pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, shallow folds, thin capsule.
- **Lingual**: base of tongue, stratified squamous epithelium, usually a single crypt each.

**MALT** is unencapsulated lymphoid tissue in the lamina propria, including GALT (gut) and BALT (bronchi). **Peyer's patches** in the ileum extend into the submucosa. They are covered by follicle-associated epithelium containing **M cells**, which transport antigens to underlying dendritic cells and lymphocytes. The resulting immune response is dominated by **IgA**, which is secreted onto the mucosa.
levels.phd:
**Thymic stromal architecture and selection.** The thymic epithelium arises from third pharyngeal pouch endoderm, with neural crest-derived mesenchyme forming the capsule. Development depends on the transcription factor **FOXN1**. Loss of FOXN1 causes the athymic "nude" phenotype, seen in mice and in rare human cases. Lymphoid progenitors from bone marrow enter at the corticomedullary junction and migrate outward as CD4-CD8- double-negative cells. They pass through DN1-DN4 stages, rearrange TCRβ, test it through the pre-TCR (β-selection) and become CD4+CD8+ double-positive cortical thymocytes.

Cortical TECs express a specialized proteasome subunit, **β5t (PSMB11)**, plus thymus-specific serine protease and cathepsin L. Together these generate a distinctive set of self-peptides on MHC for **positive selection**. Thymocytes that fail to receive signals die by neglect; estimates indicate over 90% of thymocytes never leave the thymus. Selected cells commit to CD4 or CD8 lineage and migrate medullarily under CCR7 guidance.

In the medulla, **AIRE** (autoimmune regulator) drives promiscuous expression of thousands of tissue-restricted antigens, such as insulin, in mTECs. FEZF2 controls an additional set. These antigens are presented directly by mTECs or transferred to dendritic cells, mediating **negative selection** and diversion into FOXP3+ regulatory T cells. AIRE mutations cause APECED (APS-1), a multi-organ autoimmune syndrome. Hassall's corpuscles represent terminally differentiated mTECs. They express TSLP, which conditions dendritic cells to promote Treg induction.

**Involution.** Thymic epithelial space contracts from the first year of life, accelerating after puberty under sex-steroid influence, with expansion of perivascular adipose tissue. Output persists at low levels, measurable by **T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs)**, episomal DNA by-products of TCRα rearrangement that dilute with peripheral division.

**MALT.** M cells, induced by RANKL signaling and the transcription factor Spi-B, have a short apical glycocalyx and a basolateral pocket that houses lymphocytes. They transcytose particulate antigens and microbes. Germinal centers in Peyer's patches drive class switching to IgA via TGF-β and APRIL. IgA-committed plasmablasts home to the lamina propria via α4β7–MAdCAM-1 and CCR9/CCL25. Their dimeric IgA is secreted across epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor.
levels.expert:
**Clinical histopathology of the thymus.** Thymic lesions are the most common anterior mediastinal masses in adults. **Thymomas** are neoplasms of thymic epithelium with variable admixed nonneoplastic thymocytes. The WHO classification (types A, AB, B1, B2, B3) grades them by epithelial morphology and lymphocyte richness. Thymic carcinoma is distinct and more aggressive. Many thymomas lack AIRE expression in their epithelium, which helps explain the strong link with **myasthenia gravis** (roughly 30-50% of thymoma patients). Separately, in early-onset acetylcholine-receptor-antibody myasthenia, the thymus often shows **follicular hyperplasia** with germinal centers, which the normal thymus lacks. The MGTX trial showed that thymectomy improves outcomes in nonthymomatous generalized myasthenia. A practical pitfall is **rebound thymic hyperplasia** after chemotherapy or stress, which can mimic recurrence on imaging.

**Congenital and acquired thymic failure.** DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome involves third and fourth pouch maldevelopment. Complete athymia is rare and has been treated by implanting cultured allogeneic thymus tissue (approved by the FDA in 2021). Newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency quantifies **TRECs** from dried blood spots, a direct translation of thymic biology into public health. After hematopoietic stem cell transplant or in older adults, poor thymic output limits T-cell receptor diversity. Strategies to boost regeneration, including IL-22, BMP4, sex-steroid ablation and engineered thymic organoids, remain investigational.

**Tonsils and MALT in practice.** Recurrent tonsillitis and obstructive sleep apnea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy are major indications for surgery in children. On tonsillectomy specimens, pathologists check for asymmetric enlargement, which raises concern for lymphoma. Tonsillar crypt epithelium is the classic site of **HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma**, often detected using p16 immunostaining.

**MALT lymphoma** (extranodal marginal zone lymphoma) often arises in mucosa that has *acquired* lymphoid tissue through chronic stimulation: the stomach in *Helicobacter pylori* infection, the salivary glands in Sjögren syndrome, and the thyroid in Hashimoto thyroiditis. The hallmark histologic finding is the **lymphoepithelial lesion**, in which tumor cells invade glands. Many gastric cases regress after *H. pylori* eradication, unless the tumor carries t(11;18). Open questions include how to make durable mucosal vaccines that exploit M-cell uptake.

keyPoints: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where T cells mature; tonsils and MALT are secondary
Thymic lobules have a dark cortex for positive selection and a pale medulla for negative selection
Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla identify the thymus; it lacks lymphoid follicles
AIRE lets medullary epithelium display tissue antigens to delete self-reactive T cells
Palatine tonsils have stratified squamous epithelium with deep crypts; adenoids are respiratory epithelium
Peyer's patches use M cells to sample antigen and drive IgA responses

test.q: Which structure is the classic identifier of the thymus on a slide?
test.explain: Hassall's corpuscles, concentric epithelial whorls in the medulla, are unique to the thymus. Germinal centers are typical of secondary lymphoid organs, not the normal thymus.

test.q: Where in the thymic lobule does positive selection mainly occur?
test.explain: Double-positive thymocytes in the cortex are tested on cortical epithelial cells for weak self-MHC binding.

test.q: The supporting meshwork of the thymus is formed mainly by:
test.explain: Unlike lymph nodes and spleen, which rely on reticular fibers, the thymus is built on an epithelial cell meshwork.

test.q: Which feature is ABSENT from the normal thymus?
test.explain: The normal thymus has no follicles or afferent lymphatics, which distinguishes it from lymph nodes.

test.q: The palatine tonsils are covered by:
test.explain: Palatine tonsils face the oral cavity and have nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The pharyngeal tonsil has pseudostratified ciliated epithelium.

test.q: What is the role of M cells in Peyer's patches?
test.explain: M cells transcytose antigens from the gut lumen to dendritic cells and lymphocytes beneath them.

test.q: Which antibody class dominates MALT responses?
test.explain: Mucosal immunity relies on secreted IgA, which is transported onto mucosal surfaces.

test.q: What does the blood-thymus barrier protect?
choices: Mature T cells in the blood
test.explain: The cortical barrier limits exposure of developing thymocytes to circulating antigens.

test.q: With age, the thymus undergoes involution, meaning its tissue is:
test.explain: After puberty, thymic tissue progressively shrinks and is replaced by fat, though some T-cell output persists.

test.q: The ring of tonsils around the throat is called ___ ring.
test.explain: Waldeyer's ring includes the palatine, pharyngeal and lingual tonsils.

test.q: What are the lymphoid aggregates in the ileum called?
test.explain: Peyer's patches are the classic example of gut-associated lymphoid tissue.

test.q: Deep pits in the palatine tonsil surface epithelium are called ___.
test.explain: Crypts increase surface area and trap material for immune sampling.

kidTest.q: What does the thymus do?
choices: Trains T cells to fight germs
kidTest.explain: The thymus is a school where T cells learn.

kidTest.q: Where are your tonsils?
choices: At the back of your throat
kidTest.explain: Tonsils guard the throat, where food and air come in.

kidTest.q: What happens to the thymus as you grow up?
kidTest.explain: The thymus is biggest in kids and shrinks over time.

kidTest.q: What does MALT do in your gut?
kidTest.explain: MALT works like tiny guard posts in your gut and airways.

kidTest.q: The germ-fighter training school in your chest is called the t _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The thymus is where T cells go to learn which things to attack.

advancedTest.q: A child with an AIRE mutation would most likely develop:
choices: Failure of positive selection in the cortex
Loss of IgA class switching in the gut
advancedTest.explain: Without AIRE, medullary epithelial cells cannot display tissue-restricted antigens, so self-reactive T cells escape deletion (APECED). Absent thymic epithelium fits FOXN1 loss instead.

advancedTest.q: Why do low TREC levels in a newborn signal possible SCID?
choices: TRECs measure the number of thymic epithelial cells
TRECs mark recent T-cell output from the thymus
TRECs come from B cells undergoing class switching
TRECs rise when germinal centers form in tonsils
advancedTest.explain: TRECs are by-products of TCR rearrangement in new thymic emigrants. Few TRECs means little thymic T-cell production.

advancedTest.q: A thymus resected from a young adult with myasthenia gravis shows germinal centers. This is best interpreted as:
choices: Type A thymoma of the epithelium
advancedTest.explain: The normal thymus lacks follicles, so germinal centers indicate follicular hyperplasia, typical of early-onset myasthenia.

advancedTest.q: Gastric MALT lymphoma often regresses after H. pylori treatment because:
choices: Stomach MALT is a normal tissue that is removed
Antibiotics are toxic to lymphoma cells in the stomach
The bacteria directly produce the malignant lymphocytes
The tumor arises in lymphoid tissue driven by chronic infection
advancedTest.explain: The stomach normally lacks organized lymphoid tissue. H. pylori induces it, and removing the antigenic drive can remove the growth stimulus, except in t(11;18) tumors.
